turns.assistant: Yes, that's correct, as long as the commit hasn't been pushed. `git branch feature` creates the branch at your current HEAD (with the commit), then `git reset --hard origin/main` moves main back to the remote state. Any uncommitted changes in your working directory will be lost with --hard, so stash or commit them first.

turns.assistant: Yes. Run `git stash` first (or `git stash -u` if there are untracked files you want to keep), do the branch and reset, then switch to the feature branch and `git stash pop` if the changes belong there. Or if they belong on main, pop them after the reset.

turns.user: will stash pop work on a different branch than where i stashed
turns.assistant: Yes. A stash isn't tied to a branch. It applies to whatever you have checked out, as long as the changes don't conflict with that branch's files. If there's a conflict, git tells you and keeps the stash so you can resolve it.

turns.user: ok so order: stash, branch feature, reset hard, checkout feature, stash pop
turns.assistant:
Right. That order works:

```
git stash
git branch feature
git reset --hard origin/main
git checkout feature
git stash pop
```

If `git status` shows main matching origin/main after the reset, you're good.

If you're the only user and it's your own repo, `git push --force-with-lease` is acceptable.
